message.content:
Below is a concise, practical guide to the key rights you have as a residential tenant in Texas.  (This is not legal advice; if you have a specific dispute, consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.)

| # | Right | What it means for you | Typical Texas law / statute |
|---|-------|-----------------------|-----------------------------|
| **1** | **Right to a written lease (if you sign one)** | A lease must spell out the rent amount, due date, security‑deposit limits, lease term, and any rules that are not illegal. | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |
| **2** | **Right to a safe, habitable home** | Landlord must keep the premises in good repair, free of health hazards, and compliant with building codes. | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |
| **3** | **Right to privacy** | Landlord may enter only with 24‑hour notice (or less in emergencies). | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |
| **4** | **Right to a security deposit** | Deposit ≤ 1 × monthly rent (unless the lease says otherwise). Landlord must return it within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |
| **5** | **Right to a written notice of rent increase** | If you’re on a month‑to‑month lease, landlord must give 30‑day notice before raising rent. | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |
| **6** | **Right to a written notice of lease termination** | For month‑to‑month, 30‑day notice required. For fixed‑term, landlord must give notice only if they intend to terminate early. | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |
| **7** | **Right to a fair eviction process** | Landlord must follow the proper legal steps: written notice (30 days for nonpayment, 60 days for other reasons), court filing, and a hearing. | Texas Property Code §§ 92.002–92.004 |
| **8** | **Right to dispute unlawful deductions** | If landlord keeps part of your deposit, you can file a claim in small‑claims court (≤ $20,000). | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |
| **9** | **Right to a copy of the lease** | Landlord must provide a copy of the lease upon request. | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |
| **10** | **Right to be free from discrimination** | Landlord cannot refuse to rent or charge more based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, family status, or source of income. | Texas Fair Housing Act (state & federal) |
| **11** | **Right to a reasonable repair timeline** | Landlord must fix major repairs within a reasonable time; if they fail, you may withhold rent or repair & deduct (but only for certain repairs). | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |
| **12** | **Right to a “move‑in” inspection** | You can conduct a walk‑through at move‑in and document any existing damage. | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |
| **13** | **Right to a “move‑out” inspection** | Landlord must give you a chance to fix minor damages before deducting from your deposit. | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |
| **14** | **Right to a “no‑fault” eviction notice** | If you’re in a month‑to‑month lease and the landlord wants to end tenancy, they must give 30‑day notice. | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |
| **15** | **Right to a “no‑fault” rent increase** | Landlord can raise rent only by giving 30‑day notice; no other justification needed. | Texas Property Code § 92.001 |

---

### Quick Checklist for Tenants

1. **Read the lease carefully** – note rent, deposit, pet policy, maintenance responsibilities, and termination clauses.  
2. **Document everything** – take photos of the unit at move‑in and move‑out, keep copies of all communications.  
3. **Know your notice periods** – 30 days for rent‑increase or month‑to‑month termination; 60 days for other reasons.  
4. **Keep records of payments** – bank statements, receipts, or online payment confirmations.  
5. **Report repairs promptly** – write a formal notice (email or letter) and keep a copy.  
6. **Know your eviction timeline** – if you receive a notice, you have 30 days to respond or contest.  

---

### Resources

| Resource | What it offers | Link |
|----------|----------------|------|
| **Texas Attorney General – Tenant Rights** | State‑wide tenant‑rights guide | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/ |
| **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Information on fair housing, landlord‑tenant laws | https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us/ |
| **Texas Legal Services Center** | Free legal help for low‑income tenants | https://www.texaslegalservices.org/ |
| **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | e.g., “Houston Tenants Union,” “Austin Tenant Coalition” | Search online for your city |
| **Small‑Claims Court** | File a claim for deposit disputes | https://www.txcourts.gov/small-claims/ |
| **Texas Property Code** | Full statutory text | https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/ |

---

### Common Scenarios & How to Handle Them

| Scenario | What you can do | Why it matters |
|----------|-----------------|----------------|
| **Landlord refuses to return deposit** | File a claim in small‑claims court; provide evidence of condition and repairs. | Landlord must return deposit within 30 days. |
| **Landlord enters without notice** | Send a written complaint; you may withhold rent or seek damages. | Landlord must give 24‑hour notice. |
| **Unlawful rent increase** | Verify notice period; if missing, you may refuse to pay the increase until proper notice is given. | Landlord must give 30‑day notice. |
| **Unreasonable repair delays** | Write a formal notice; if unresolved, you may repair & deduct (for certain repairs) or withhold rent. | Landlord must keep premises habitable. |
| **Discrimination claim** | File a complaint with the Texas Attorney General or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | Discrimination is illegal. |

---

### Bottom Line

- **Security deposits** are capped at one month’s rent and must be returned within 30 days.  
- **Notice requirements** are strict: 24 hrs for entry, 30 days for rent increases or month‑to‑month termination, 60 days for other terminations.  
- **Habitability** is a legal requirement; landlords must maintain the property.  
- **Eviction** must follow the formal legal process; landlords cannot evict you without a court order.  

If you encounter a problem that you can’t resolve on your own, reach out to a local tenant‑rights group or an attorney who specializes in landlord‑tenant law.
